citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A subset $S\subseteq R$ is **multiplicative** if $1\in S$ and $s,t\in S$ implies $st\in S$.

On $R\times S$, define
$$ (r,s)\sim(r',s')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u(rs'-r's)=0\text{ for some }u\in S. $$
The **localisation** of $R$ at $S$, denoted $S^{-1}R$, is the set of equivalence classes for this relation. The class of $(r,s)$ is written $r/s$, and its arithmetic is
$$ \frac r s+\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rs'+r's}{ss'},\qquad \frac r s\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rr'}{ss'}. $$
The **localisation map** is the ring homomorphism
$$ \lambda_S:R\longrightarrow S^{-1}R,\qquad r\longmapsto r/1. $$
Every $s\in S$ maps to a unit, with $(s/1)^{-1}=1/s$. The construction permits $0\in S$; in that case the localisation is the zero ring.

Fix $m\ge1$. Two holomorphic functions on neighbourhoods of
$0\in\mathbb C^m$ ([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]])
are **equivalent at $0$** when they agree on some smaller neighbourhood of $0$.
An equivalence class is a **holomorphic germ at $0$**, and the set of all such
germs is denoted $\mathcal O_{m,0}$.

For the $m=1$ boundary case used later, also set
$$\mathcal O_{0,0}:=\mathbb C,\qquad \mathfrak m_{0,0}:=\{0\}.$$
This is the ring of constant germs at the unique point of $\mathbb C^0$.

If $[f]$ and $[g]$ are germs, choose representatives defined on a common
neighbourhood of $0$ and set

$$[f]+[g]:=[f+g],\qquad [f][g]:=[fg].$$

These are well defined because agreement on a smaller neighbourhood is
preserved by pointwise addition and multiplication. Thus $\mathcal O_{m,0}$ is a
commutative ring with identity $[1]$.

Its distinguished ideal is

$$\mathfrak m_{m,0}:=\{[f]\in\mathcal O_{m,0}:f(0)=0\}.$$

This is well defined because equivalent representatives have the same value at
$0$. The local-ring terminology used later is that of [[def-local-ring]].

Fix $a \in \mathbb C$, and let $\mathcal O_a$ be the set of holomorphic germs at
$a$. Define

$$[f]_a + [g]_a := [f+g]_a,\qquad [f]_a[g]_a := [fg]_a.$$

Then $\mathcal O_a$ is a commutative ring with identity $[1]_a$. A germ
$[f]_a \in \mathcal O_a$ is a unit if and only if $f(a) \ne 0$. Consequently

$$\mathfrak m_a := \{[f]_a \in \mathcal O_a : f(a)=0\}$$

is the unique maximal ideal, so $\mathcal O_a$ is a local ring.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $[f]\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$. Then $[f]$ is a unit in
$\mathcal O_{m,0}$ if and only if $f(0)\ne0$. Consequently
$\mathcal O_{m,0}$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_{m,0}$.

For every integer $m\ge1$, the holomorphic germ ring $\mathcal O_{m,0}$ is a
Noetherian commutative ring.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and let $r$ be a polyradius. Suppose
$c,c':\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ both satisfy a bound
$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$ and
$|c'_\alpha|\le M'\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$, and suppose

$$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha=\sum_\alpha c'_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha \qquad\text{for every }z\in\Delta_r(a).$$

Then $c_\alpha=c'_\alpha$ for every multi-index $\alpha$. In particular a
function has at most one such power-series representation about a given centre,
and its coefficients are $\partial^\alpha_zf(a)/\alpha!$.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then the iterated polynomial ring
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of [[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] is
Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$.

The index starts at $0$, where the published definition sets
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]=R$ and the assertion is the hypothesis itself.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then

1. $R/I$ is Noetherian for every ideal $I$ of $R$
   ([[def-quotient-ring]]), and
2. $S^{-1}R$ is Noetherian for every multiplicative subset $S\subseteq R$
   ([[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).

Both cases include their degenerate instances: $I=R$ makes $R/I$ the zero ring,
and $0\in S$ makes $S^{-1}R$ the zero ring, and the zero ring is Noetherian.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $I \subseteq R$ be an ideal, and let
$N \subseteq M$ be finitely generated $R$-modules.

1. The natural map
   $$    \widehat M/\widehat N \longrightarrow \widehat{M/N}    $$
   is an isomorphism.
2. Under the natural map $\widehat N \to \widehat M$, the image of
   $\widehat N$ is the $\widehat R$-submodule $N\widehat R \subseteq \widehat M$.
   In particular, for every ideal $J \subseteq R$,
   $$    \widehat{JM}\cong J\widehat M.    $$
3. For every $n \ge 0$,
   $$    \widehat M/I^n\widehat M \cong M/I^nM.    $$

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Assume dependent choice, as available under the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication $3\Rightarrow4$ uses dependent choice. The implications
$1\Leftrightarrow2$, $2\Rightarrow3$, and $4\Rightarrow2$ are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

derivations.claim: AC implies DC. For a nonempty set $Y$ with a serial relation $R$, the successor sets $\{z\in Y:yRz\}$ are nonempty; [A1] chooses one successor for each such set. This defines a self-map $s:Y\to Y$ with $yRs(y)$, and [F10] recursively generates a sequence from any specified starting point.

For each $k\ge1$, every $s\in P\setminus\mathfrak m$ has the form $s=c(1+h)$ with $c=s(0)\ne0$ and $h\in\mathfrak m$. Modulo $\mathfrak m^k$, $h^k=0$, so $c^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-h)^j$ is an inverse for $s$. Thus localization changes no $k$-jet and $A_0/\mathfrak m^kA_0\cong P/\mathfrak m^k$. The quotient $P/\mathfrak m^k$ records precisely the coefficients of monomials of total degree less than $k$, and its transition maps discard coefficients of degree at least the new truncation order. In a compatible sequence, the coefficient of each $w^\alpha$ is therefore stable at every stage $k>|\alpha|$, giving an array in $T$; conversely, every array in $T$ gives these compatible truncations. The induced addition is pointwise, and multiplication is the finite convolution in the Statement, so this is a ring isomorphism. Hence $\widehat{A_0}\cong T$.

Every germ in $\mathfrak n$ has a power series with no constant term by [F6]. Assign each nonconstant monomial to the first coordinate with positive exponent; grouping the terms by that coordinate writes the germ as $\sum_{i=1}^n w_i g_i$, where each $g_i$ converges on a smaller polydisc by absolute convergence. Hence $\mathfrak n=(w_1,\ldots,w_n)$.

By [F11], every ideal of $\mathbb C$ is finitely generated; the DC-dependent ideal characterization in [F11], using DC from step 1.1, makes $\mathbb C$ Noetherian. The finite-variable corollary in [F8] then makes $P$ Noetherian, and [F8] makes its localization $A_0$ Noetherian under the same DC. The ring $A_0$ is local: fractions with numerator outside $\mathfrak m$ are units, while the residue map $p/q\mapsto p(0)/q(0)$ is a surjective homomorphism to $\mathbb C$ with kernel $\mathfrak m A_0$. The ring $H$ is Noetherian by [F5] and local by [F3] when $n=1$ and by [F4] for every $n$. Since $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$ and every element of $I$ vanishes at the origin, $IA_0$ and $IH$ lie in the respective maximal ideals. Their quotients are therefore Noetherian local rings, with maximal ideals the images of those ambient maximal ideals.

For $k\ge1$, truncate the unique Taylor series from [F6] to total degree less than $k$. This gives a surjection $H\to P/\mathfrak m^k$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ of degree at least $k$, assign the first monomial divisor $w^\beta$ in a fixed ordering among the finitely many divisors of total degree $k$; grouping the absolutely convergent subseries by the finitely many possible $\beta$ writes the tail as $\sum_{|\beta|=k}w^\beta g_\beta$. Thus the kernel is contained in $\mathfrak n^k$. Conversely, step 1.3 makes $\mathfrak n^k$ generated by the degree-$k$ coordinate monomials. To apply [F7], choose a polydisc about $0$ with positive radii whose closure lies inside a common convergence polydisc for a finite expression of an element of $\mathfrak n^k$ as a sum of degree-$k$ monomials times germs. By [F6], the Taylor coefficients of each germ are uniformly bounded on these radii; multiplying by a fixed monomial shifts the coefficient indices and preserves a bound of the same form, and the finite sum preserves such a bound. The Taylor series of the given element has the same kind of bound by [F6]. The two sums agree on the chosen polydisc, so [F7] applies and shows that all coefficients of total degree below $k$ vanish. Hence $\mathfrak n^k$ lies in the kernel, and $H/\mathfrak n^k\cong P/\mathfrak m^k$.

Taking inverse limits in steps 1.2 and 2.2 identifies $\widehat{A_0}$ and $\widehat H$ with $T$. Each polynomial variable maps to the same formal variable under both completion maps, so the induced map $\widehat{A_0}\to\widehat H$ is the identity of $T$.

Under the assumed AC, apply [F9] to the finitely generated ideals $IA_0\subseteq A_0$ and $IH\subseteq H$; these rings are Noetherian by step 2.1. Their images in $T$ are both generated by the same finite polynomial generators of $I$, because the maps in step 3.1 send each $w_i$ to the same formal variable. Thus $\widehat{A_I}\cong T/IT\cong\widehat{H_I}$, and the induced map on completions is the identity under these identifications. The quotient is by $I$ itself, not by its radical.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **scheme** is a locally ringed space $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ such that every
point has an open neighbourhood which, with the restricted structure sheaf, is
an affine scheme. The empty locally ringed space is consequently a scheme.

A morphism $f:X\to S$ is **locally of finite type** if every point of $X$ has
an affine open neighbourhood $U$ and $f(U)$ lies in an affine open
$V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $S$ such that $U=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and
$A\to B$ is of finite type. It is **of finite type** if it is locally of finite
type and quasi-compact.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra with
structure map $\eta_A\colon R\to A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

**The subalgebra generated by finitely many elements.** Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and
$a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Iterating the universal property of a polynomial ring
([[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring]]) along the recursion
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}]=R[x_1,\ldots,x_k][x_{k+1}]$ of
[[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] gives a unique unital ring
homomorphism

$$\operatorname{ev}\colon R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\longrightarrow A$$

that agrees with $\eta_A$ on constants and sends $x_i$ to $a_i$ for each $i$;
at each step of the recursion the one-variable universal property supplies
existence and uniqueness of the extension, and at $n=0$ the map is $\eta_A$
itself. Its image is written $R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ and is called the
**$R$-subalgebra of $A$ generated by $a_1,\ldots,a_n$**. It is a subring of $A$
containing $\eta_A(R)$, and it is the smallest such subring containing
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, since any subring with those properties is closed under the
sums and products that make up a polynomial expression. At $n=0$ it is
$\eta_A(R)$, the image of $R$ in $A$.

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

**Module-finite.** $A$ is **module-finite over $R$**, equivalently a **finite
$R$-algebra**, when $A$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]) for the action
$r\cdot a=\eta_A(r)a$.

**Module-finite implies finite type.** If $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ generate $A$ as an
$R$-module then $R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$, being a subring of $A$ that contains
$\eta_A(R)$ and every $b_i$, contains every $R$-linear combination
$\sum_i\eta_A(r_i)b_i$ and hence all of $A$; so $A=R[b_1,\ldots,b_n]$. The
converse fails, and the companion examples page carries a witness.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then the iterated polynomial ring
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of [[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] is
Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$.

The index starts at $0$, where the published definition sets
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]=R$ and the assertion is the hypothesis itself.

Assume dependent choice, as available under the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The following are equivalent.

1. $R$ is Noetherian ([[def-noetherian-ring]]).
2. Every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated: for every ideal $\mathfrak a$ there
   are finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$, with $n\in\mathbb N$, such
   that $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.
3. **Ascending chain condition.** Every chain of ideals
   $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\mathfrak a_2\subseteq\cdots$
   indexed by $\mathbb N$ stabilises: there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with
   $\mathfrak a_n=\mathfrak a_N$ for every $n\ge N$.
4. **Maximal condition.** Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal
   member with respect to inclusion.

The implication $3\Rightarrow4$ uses dependent choice. The implications
$1\Leftrightarrow2$, $2\Rightarrow3$, and $4\Rightarrow2$ are choice-free. The same
attribution is carried by
[[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules]], from which this
statement is obtained.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put
$P=\mathbb C[w_1,\ldots,w_n]$, and let $\mathfrak m=(w_1,\ldots,w_n)$.
Let $A_0=P_{\mathfrak m}$ be the localization at the polynomials nonzero at
the origin, let $H=\mathbb C\{w_1,\ldots,w_n\}$ be the ring of holomorphic
function germs at the origin, and let $T$ be the set of coefficient arrays
$a=(a_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^n}\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb N^n}$, written
$\sum_\alpha a_\alpha w^\alpha$ where $w^\alpha=\prod_{i=1}^n w_i^{\alpha_i}$,
with pointwise addition and multiplication
defined by $(ab)_\alpha=\sum_{\beta+\gamma=\alpha}a_\beta b_\gamma$. These
operations make $T$ a commutative unital ring: each convolution is finite, its
multiplicative identity has coefficient $1$ at $\alpha=0$ and $0$ elsewhere,
and no convergence condition is imposed; this
ring is denoted $\mathbb C\llbracket w_1,\ldots,w_n\rrbracket$. For
each polynomial in $P$, its finitely supported coefficient array defines the
canonical ring map $P\to T$; for an ideal $I\subseteq P$, $IT$ denotes the ideal
of $T$ generated by its image under this map. For any finitely generated ideal
$I\subseteq
\mathfrak m$, set $A_I=A_0/IA_0$ and $H_I=H/IH$. For a local ring $R$ with
maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_R$, define its completion by
$\widehat R=\varprojlim_{k\ge1}R/\mathfrak m_R^k$.

The polynomial-to-germ map induces a local homomorphism $A_I\to H_I$. The
four rings $A_0,H,A_I,H_I$ are Noetherian local rings, and the induced map on
completions identifies both $\widehat{A_I}$ and $\widehat{H_I}$ canonically
with $T/IT$. In particular, the comparison uses the same extended defining
ideal $I$ and does not replace it by its radical, so nilpotent classes are
retained.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring, and let $\widehat R$ be its
$\mathfrak m$-adic completion.

1. $\widehat R$ is a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal
   $\mathfrak m\widehat R$.
2. The residue field is unchanged:
   $$    \widehat R/\mathfrak m\widehat R \cong R/\mathfrak m.    $$
3. The completion map $R \to \widehat R$ is faithfully flat.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $I \subseteq R$ be an ideal. Then the
completion map
$$ R \to \widehat R $$
makes $\widehat R$ into a flat $R$-module.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M$ be an $R$-module. The following are equivalent:

1. $M$ is flat.
2. For every injection $K\hookrightarrow N$, the induced map $K\otimes_RM\to N\otimes_RM$ is injective.
3. For every ideal $I\subseteq R$, the multiplication map $I\otimes_RM\to M$, $a\otimes m\mapsto am$, is injective.
4. The map in claim 3 is injective for every finitely generated ideal $I$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M$ be an $R$-module. The module $M$ is **flat** if the functor $-\otimes_RM$ preserves exact sequences: whenever $A\to B\to C$ is exact, so is

$$A\otimes_RM\longrightarrow B\otimes_RM\longrightarrow C\otimes_RM.$$

Since tensoring is always right exact ([[thm-right-exactness-of-tensor-products]], [[def-exact-and-short-exact-sequences-of-modules]]), the definition asks for the remaining left-hand exactness. Its equivalent formulation as preservation of injections is proved separately rather than built into the definition.

The module $M$ is **faithfully flat** if a sequence of $R$-modules is exact exactly when its tensor with $M$ is exact.

For a unital ring homomorphism $f:R\to S$ ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) between commutative rings, $S$ is an $R$-module by $r\cdot s=f(r)s$. The map $f$ is **flat**, respectively **faithfully flat**, when this $R$-module is flat, respectively faithfully flat.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the prime and maximal ideal existence used in the
spectral reformulations.

Let $f:R\to S$ be a flat homomorphism of commutative rings. The following are
equivalent:

1. $f$ is faithfully flat.
2. For every proper ideal $I\subsetneq R$, the extended ideal $IS$ is proper.
3. Every maximal ideal of $R$ has a prime ideal of $S$ lying over it.
4. The map on prime spectra
   $$    \operatorname{Spec}(S)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)    $$
   is surjective.

Assume Dependent Choice (DC). For a short exact sequence
$0\to N'\to N\to N''\to0$ of right $R$-modules and a left module $M$
with a supplied projective resolution, there is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(N',M)\to\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(N,M)\to\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(N'',M)\xrightarrow{\partial_i}\operatorname{Tor}_{i-1}^R(N',M)\to\cdots.$$
Its degree-zero tail is
$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N'',M)\xrightarrow{\partial_1}N'\otimes_R M\to N\otimes_R M\to N''\otimes_R M\to0.$$
The sequence is natural in morphisms of short exact sequences and in maps
of left modules equipped with projective resolutions. Tor can be computed
using that left resolution, or using the balanced identification whenever
resolutions on the other side are supplied.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice and supplied projective-resolution data.
A right $R$-module $N$ is flat if and only if $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)=0$ for every left $R$-module $M$.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element is represented by a unique finitely supported coefficient family $(r_x)_{x\in X}$, and is written
$$\sum_{x\in X}r_xe_x.$$
The **standard basis map** $X\to R^{(X)}$ sends $x$ to $e_x$. It is injective exactly when $1_R\ne0$ or $X$ has at most one element; in these cases it is the standard basis inclusion. Indeed, for distinct $x,y$ the $x$-coordinates of $e_x$ and $e_y$ are $1_R$ and $0$. For the zero ring every $e_x$ is zero, but the indexed family $(e_x)_{x\in X}$ still has unique finitely supported coefficients.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $X$ a set, and $M$ a left $R$-module. Every set map $u:X\to M$ extends uniquely to an $R$-module homomorphism $\bar u:R^{(X)}\to M$ satisfying $\bar u(e_x)=u(x)$. Explicitly,
$$\bar u\left(\sum_{x\in F}r_xe_x\right)=\sum_{x\in F}r_xu(x).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A subset $S\subseteq R$ is **multiplicative** if $1\in S$ and $s,t\in S$ implies $st\in S$.

On $R\times S$, define
$$ (r,s)\sim(r',s')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u(rs'-r's)=0\text{ for some }u\in S. $$
The **localisation** of $R$ at $S$, denoted $S^{-1}R$, is the set of equivalence classes for this relation. The class of $(r,s)$ is written $r/s$, and its arithmetic is
$$ \frac r s+\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rs'+r's}{ss'},\qquad \frac r s\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rr'}{ss'}. $$
The **localisation map** is the ring homomorphism
$$ \lambda_S:R\longrightarrow S^{-1}R,\qquad r\longmapsto r/1. $$
Every $s\in S$ maps to a unit, with $(s/1)^{-1}=1/s$. The construction permits $0\in S$; in that case the localisation is the zero ring.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a scheme of finite type over $\mathbb C$
and let $x\in X$ be a closed point with residue field $\mathbb C$. Choose an
affine neighborhood of $x$ presented as (adding a dummy coordinate if needed)
$\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb C[w_1,\ldots,w_n]/I)$, with $n\ge1$, $I$ a
finitely generated polynomial ideal contained in $(w_1,\ldots,w_n)$, and $x$
the origin. Write
$A=(\mathbb C[w_1,\ldots,w_n]_{(w_1,\ldots,w_n)})/I\mathbb C[w_1,\ldots,w_n]_{(w_1,\ldots,w_n)}$.
On this chart, define the analytic local ring by extending the same ideal to
holomorphic germs,
$B=\mathbb C\{w_1,\ldots,w_n\}/I\mathbb C\{w_1,\ldots,w_n\}$; this quotient
retains the given scheme structure, including nilpotents. For a local ring $R$
with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_R$, let
$\widehat R=\varprojlim_{k\ge1}R/\mathfrak m_R^k$.

The canonical local homomorphism $A\to B$, which sends each polynomial class
to the same holomorphic germ, is injective and faithfully flat.
Its induced map $\widehat A\to\widehat B$ is an isomorphism, with both
completions canonically identified with
$\mathbb C\llbracket w_1,\ldots,w_n\rrbracket/I\mathbb C\llbracket w_1,\ldots,w_n\rrbracket$. For every
$A$-module $M$, the map $M\to M\otimes_A B$ is injective, and the quotient
$B/A$ is a flat $A$-module. These are local-ring conclusions; no relative
direct-image comparison is asserted.

Let $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and let $r$ be a polyradius. Suppose
$c,c':\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ both satisfy a bound
$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$ and
$|c'_\alpha|\le M'\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$, and suppose

$$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha=\sum_\alpha c'_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha \qquad\text{for every }z\in\Delta_r(a).$$

Then $c_\alpha=c'_\alpha$ for every multi-index $\alpha$. In particular a
function has at most one such power-series representation about a given centre,
and its coefficients are $\partial^\alpha_zf(a)/\alpha!$.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$, a polyradius $r$, a real $M\ge0$ and
coefficients $c:\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ with

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}\qquad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha.$$

Then:

1. for every $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
   $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
   $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$, so its sum $g$ is defined on
   $\Delta_r(a)$;
2. $g$ is holomorphic on $\Delta_r(a)$, with
   $$Dg(z)h=\sum_{k<m}b_k(z)h_k,\qquad b_k(z)=\sum_{\alpha}\alpha_k\,c_\alpha(z-a)^{\alpha-e_k},$$
   the $k$th series running over the multi-indices with $\alpha_k\ge1$ and
   converging absolutely on $\Delta_r(a)$; equivalently
   $\partial_{z_k}g=b_k$;
3. for every $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the derived coefficients
   $\alpha_kc_\alpha$, re-indexed as a power series, obey a bound of the same
   shape on the polyradius $\theta r$, so the differentiation may be iterated;
   and every iterated complex partial derivative
   $\partial^\beta_zg:=\partial_{z_0}^{\beta_0}\cdots\partial_{z_{m-1}}^{\beta_{m-1}}g$
   exists on $\Delta_r(a)$ with
   $$\partial^\beta_zg(a)=\beta!\,c_\beta .$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[t]$ and its closed point $t=0$. It gives faithful flatness of $A\to B$ and identifies both maximal-ideal completions with $\mathbb C\llbracket t\rrbracket$.

Fix any $R>0$ and put $u_n=R^n/n!$. Choose $N$ with $N+1\ge2R$. For every $k\ge0$, $u_{N+k+1}/u_{N+k}=R/(N+k+1)\le1/2$, so induction gives $u_{N+k}\le u_N2^{-k}$. The finite identity $\sum_{k=0}^K2^{-k}=2-2^{-K}\le2$ bounds every partial sum of the tail by $2u_N$. Define the explicit finite constant $M_R=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}u_n+2u_N$, with an empty initial sum interpreted as zero. For $n<N$, $u_n$ is one nonnegative summand of $M_R$; for $n\ge N$, the geometric estimate gives $u_n\le u_N\le M_R$. Thus $R^n/n!\le M_R$ for every $n$, without passing to an infinite sum; hence for any $0<r<R$, $1/n!\le M_RR^{-n}\le M_Rr^{-n}$. The coefficient family of $e(t)$ therefore satisfies the exact uniform bound required by [F4] on radius $r$, so [F4] makes its sum holomorphic on $|t|<r$. As $R$ is arbitrary, these disks cover a neighborhood of $0$ (indeed all of $\mathbb C$), and $e$ defines a holomorphic germ.

Suppose $e(t)=p(t)/q(t)$ in $A$, with $q(0)
e0$. Then $q(t)e(t)=p(t)$ as germs and evaluation at $0$ gives $p(0)=q(0)
e0$. Write $q(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}q_jt^j$ with $q_d
e0$, and let $m=\deg p$. Equality of germs supplies $\varepsilon>0$ such that $qe=p$ on $|t|<\varepsilon$. Fix $R>0$ and choose $0<r<\min(R,\varepsilon)$. By step 1.2 the coefficients $c_n=1/n!$ of $e$ satisfy $|c_n|\le M_Rr^{-n}$. The coefficient $b_N=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,N)}q_jc_{N-j}$ of $qe$ satisfies $|b_N|\le M_Rr^{-N}\sum_{j=0}^d|q_j|r^j$. If $p_N$ denotes the coefficient of $t^N$ in $p$, then $|p_N|\le M_pr^{-N}$ for all $N$, where $M_p=\max_{0\le N\le m}|p_N|r^N$. Thus both series satisfy the common-radius bound in [F3], and their sums agree on $|t|<r$, so [F3] gives $b_N=p_N$ for every $N$. For every integer $N>\max(d,m)$ this yields $\sum_{j=0}^{d}q_j/(N-j)!=0$. Multiplying by $N!$ gives $Q(N)=0$, where $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}q_j z(z-1)\cdots(z-j+1)$. This is a nonzero polynomial of degree $d$ with leading coefficient $q_d$. To prove the needed root bound locally, a nonzero constant has no roots. If a degree-$d$ polynomial $P$ with $d>0$ has a root $a$, the finite identities $z^j-a^j=(z-a)\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}z^{j-1-\ell}a^\ell$ give $P(z)=P(z)-P(a)=(z-a)S(z)$, where $S$ has degree $d-1$ and the same nonzero leading coefficient. Every other root $b
e a$ satisfies $(b-a)S(b)=0$, hence $S(b)=0$ because the nonzero complex number $b-a$ is invertible. Induction gives at most $d-1$ such roots and at most $d$ roots in total. Applying this bound to $Q$ contradicts its vanishing on the infinitely many distinct integers $N>\max(d,m)$. This contradiction proves that $e(t)$ is not in the image of $A$.
Step 1.1 establishes faithful flatness and equality of completions, while step 2.1 establishes failure of surjectivity.
